extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political philosophy, policymakers, legal theorists, and civil libertarians
extracted.subtask_description: Normative criteria for deciding when society (law or public opinion) may legitimately intervene in individuals' lives versus when individuals should have autonomous liberty. The page articulates principles (a harm-based distinction, duties to others vs duties to self, role of education and opinion) to delimit social authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value_of_individuality_and_diversity
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuality and the plurality of characters, classes, and nations are the source of human progress; making people all alike produces stagnation (China as warning).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preserve differences even when some deviations may not be 'for the better' because variety yields multiple valuable paths and enables mutual learning; watch social forces (education, communication, commerce, ascendancy of public opinion) that tend to assimilate people and erode individuality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessary_conditions_for_human_development
rubrics_metrics.description: Two necessary conditions of human development are freedom and variety of situations (as noted by Wilhelm von Humboldt).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy and social organization should protect both political/social freedom and diversity of circumstances; recognize that modern developments (education, communications, commerce, public opinion) can reduce situational variety and thus hinder development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allocation_of_authority_based_on_primary_interests
rubrics_metrics.description: Each of society and individuality should have that portion of life which more particularly concerns it: individuality the parts chiefly of individual concern, society the parts chiefly of social concern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the test of whose interests are primarily at stake to delimit social interference: where society's interest predominates, social authority is justified; where the individual's own interest predominates, autonomy should be preserved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Society_may_enforce_noninjury_and_equitable_contribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Society is justified in enforcing conduct that (1) prevents injuring the interests of one another (rights), and (2) secures that each person bears an equitable share of labours and sacrifices for defending the society or its members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such conditions may be enforced 'at all costs' against those who withhold fulfilment; these form the primary domain for legal coercion and sanction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harm_principle_self_regarding_vs_other_regarding
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no room for interference when a person's conduct affects no persons besides himself; in all such cases there should be perfect legal and social freedom to do the action and stand the consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish sharply between self-regarding acts (left to individual liberty) and other-regarding acts (subject to social or legal jurisdiction); protect legal and social freedom for actions that do not harm others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social_opinion_as_sanction_for_non_rights_violations
rubrics_metrics.description: When an individual's acts are hurtful to others or want due consideration but do not violate constituted rights, the offender may justly be punished by opinion though not by law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow moral censure and social penalties (ostracism, loss of esteem) for conduct that is objectionable but not legally punishable; social sanctions are appropriate short of legal punishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education_and_persuasion_over_compulsion
rubrics_metrics.description: Disinterested benevolence and education should be used to persuade people to their good rather than coercion ('whips and scourges'); education works by conviction and persuasion as well as by compulsion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize non-coercive instruments (education, exhortation, moral suasion) to promote self-regarding virtues; coercion is a last resort and often counterproductive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individual_superiority_in_knowledge_of_own_circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: Interference of society to overrule an individual's judgment in matters that concern only himself must be grounded on general presumptions which are likely to be wrong because outsiders are less acquainted with particular circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defer to the individual's superior information about his own feelings and situation; be wary of applying general presumptions to unique individual cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social_penalties_should_be_natural_consequences_not_punitive
rubrics_metrics.description: The inconveniences strictly inseparable from the unfavourable judgment of others are the only penalties to which a person should be subjected for self-regarding conduct; these are natural/spontaneous consequences, not purposely inflicted punishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permit loss of esteem, avoidance, and other natural social effects for personal faults, but refrain from deliberately inflicting additional suffering for those faults when they concern only the individual's own good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stronger_treatment_for_actions_violating_others_rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Acts that encroach on others' rights or inflict loss, falsehood, duplicity, unfair advantage, or selfish abstinence from defending others are proper objects of moral reprobation and, in grave cases, of punishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When conduct injures others or arises from dispositions (malice, envy, cruelty, dissimulation) that threaten social welfare, apply moral condemnation and appropriate legal or punitive measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duties_to_oneself_not_socially_obligatory
rubrics_metrics.description: What are called duties to ourselves (prudence, self-respect, self-development) are not socially obligatory unless circumstances render them at the same time duties to others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid making private virtues or self-regarding prudence a matter of legal or moral obligation for others unless failing them produces concrete duties or harms to third parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definite_damage_or_risk_triggers_law_or_morality
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever there is a definite damage, or a definite risk of damage, either to an individual or to the public, the case is taken out of the province of liberty and placed in that of morality or law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the presence of concrete harm or risk as the threshold for moving from tolerated liberty to enforceable norms (example: a soldier drunk on duty may be punished).

rubrics_metrics.name: Toleration_of_constructive_or_contingent_injury_for_liberty
rubrics_metrics.description: For merely contingent or constructive injury which neither violates a specific duty nor occasions perceptible hurt to any assignable individual, the inconvenience is one society can afford to bear for the greater good of human freedom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept some diffuse social costs of private behavior in order to preserve broad individual freedom, rather than criminalizing or coercing every imprudent act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsibility_of_society_for_education_before_coercion
rubrics_metrics.description: Society has the period of childhood and nonage to make the rising generation capable of rational conduct; if it lets members grow up mere children, it is to blame for consequent irrational conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize education and formative institutions to promote rational self-government; failures in upbringing do not justify extending coercive power over competent adults in their private concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid_coercion_as_counterproductive
rubrics_metrics.description: Resort to coercion in matters of personal conduct discredits and frustrates better means of influencing conduct and will provoke rebellion in the spirited and independent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that coercive measures often produce defiance and perverse outcomes; use persuasion and voluntary education to cultivate virtues instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Majoritarian_censorship_in_personal_matters_is_unreliable
rubrics_metrics.description: The opinion of an overruling majority imposed as law on the minority, on questions of self-regarding conduct, is quite as likely to be wrong as right; public censure often springs from mere distaste rather than sound judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious about letting prevailing public sentiment dictate personal conduct rules; distinguish between judgments grounded in shared interests and those based on mere dislike or intolerance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permit_individual_choice_in_uncertain_matters_except_universally_condemned
rubrics_metrics.description: Leave the freedom and choice of individuals in all uncertain matters undisturbed; only require abstention from modes of conduct which universal experience has condemned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In areas of reasonable uncertainty about best ways of living, favor individual experimentation and choice; restrict conduct only where there is overwhelming and universal experience against it.
